newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine analysts unperturbed about Bocon issues.
newsitem.headline: Argentine analysts unperturbed about Bocon issues.

text.p: Argentine analysts are eyeing the possible issue of another series of Bocon bonds to cover pension payments with subdued anticipation, arguing the new supply will be too small to push market prices down.

"I don't think this will affect the market because I do not think it will be a big issue," said Sergio Galvan, head of research at Bansud. At the most, he estimates, the issue will be some $800 million.

Following statements by officials that the government will likely issue bonds to cover part of the backdated payments to pensioners following a recent supreme court ruling, the local market has been abuzz with speculation on how large an issue would be and what impact such an issue would have on outstanding Bocon bonds.

Julio Caceres, the Economy Ministry's Coordination Secretary, has said part of the money will be raised by issuing Bocones, but he did not specify how large the issue would be nor when it would be placed.
But with the dust settling after the initial questions by market players over whether current Bocon bonds would be crowded out of the market, analysts now think the impact will be limited.

The supreme court ruled December 27 that the government will have to raise pensions by 13.8 percent for 70,000 pensioners from 1991 to 1994 in retroactive payments. The ruling re-established the mobility of pension payments since they were fixed by Convertibility in 1991.
Roberto Costa Bourdieu, senior fixed income analyst at Banco Rio reckons any issue will be about $700 million, and "will not have the same liquidity as the other Bocones."

Argentina launched two series of Bocon bonds (or consolidation bonds) with maturities of 10 and 16 years in 1991, which it used as payment to suppliers to the state and pensioners. The paper was given directly to the suppliers and pensioners, allowing them to sell the bonds in the market.
The dollar-denominated Bocon Previsional Series 2 which matures in 2001 is the local market benchmark.
Some observers think it possible that the supreme court ruling will set a precedent and pave the way for other eligible pensioners to seek compensation payments.
But, analysts say, even if that happened, any big bond issue would not likely come any time soon because this expenditure and the placement of Bocon bonds is not included in the 1997 budget.

"They (the government) will need a law" to issue new Bocon bonds, which means Congress would have to give its approval, said Hugo Diaz Lourenco, senior analyst at financial consultancy C&E Consultores. That would take time.
Economy Minister Roque Fernandez has said a law is being prepared to be sent to Congress.

Fernandez said there will be no extra funds other than those that have already been earmarked in the 1997 budget for this kind of contingency. Issuing Bocones would not affect the budget because it would delay the expenditure. The older Bocones do not start paying interest before this year, meaning any government spending has been delayed even further.
Issuing Bocones that mature in the future is a way to "avoid paying the pensioners now," said Lourenco.
Anyway, the large global bond issues announced by the government in previous days will be of larger importance to the government. "The government will focus on the other issues," said Bourdieu.

Fernandez said Tuesday Argentina is to launch a two-tranche $2.0 billion global bond, made up of a five- and a 20-year issue, to be placed in the second half of January. A further $1.0 billion will be placed before the end of March.
